newsitem.title: USA: News Corp. investment in EchoStar delayed.
newsitem.headline: News Corp. investment in EchoStar delayed.

text.p: News Corp. Ltd. has delayed a $1 billion investment in EchoStar Communications Corp., the companies said Monday, as their planned venture into the growing but competitive direct-TV satellite business showed signs of fraying.
News Corp. told EchoStar on Friday that it was setting new conditions for its agreement to make the investment, which was announced in February, Echostar said in a statement.

Industry analysts said several issues were hurting the proposed partnership, including the strong personalities of News Corp. Chairman Rupert Murdoch and EchoStar Chairman Charles Ergen, each of whom is used to being in charge.
Others said Murdoch may be having second thoughts about investing more than $1 billion in a venture that faces regulatory hurdles and intense competition inside and outside the industry.

In a brief statement, Echostar said it has delayed making filings with regulators in the United States after News Corp. asked it to abandon its system for controlling consumer access to satellite-delivered television programmes and replace it with a system provided by News Corp.

"It seems kind of odd it would be a reason," NatWest Securities analyst Gary Farber said. "It's kind of like if you're going to get married to somebody and you couldn't agree on the band so you call off the wedding."

"It's the one concrete issue they're willing to hang their hat on," said Ted Henderson, managing director of research at Janco Partners. "But they're probably more meat on the bones of the other issues."
EchoStar currently uses a system called Nagra SA to allow subscribers to view only those channels for which they have paid while News Corp. has a stake in another vendor.
"This does not seem to me to be a deal-breaker issue," Smith Barney analyst John Reidy said.
Instead, some analysts said Murdoch may be seeking improved terms from EchoStar.

When it was announced in February, the two companies said their direct-broadcast venture would offer as many as 500 channels of digital TV, Internet services and local broadcast TV signals to markets across the United States.
It was viewed as competition to DirecTV, which is owned by General Motors Corp.'s Hughes Electronics unit and AT&T Corp., as well as Primestar, owned by several cable TV operators.

"I think there are two very strong personalities with Charles and Rupert," said Bob Scherman, editor and publisher of Satellite Business News magazine. "They are both playing chicken right now. I don't know who's going to blink first."
"Murdoch and Ergen, from the day this deal came out, people were saying, 'Boy, it's hard to those guys working together,'" Janco Partners' Henderson said.

There have been recent reports that Murdoch had approached Tele-Communications Inc. Chief Executive John Malone about a possible alliance with Primestar, the satellite partnership made up of six companies.

News Corp. spokesman Jim Platt would not comment on those reports or on EchoStar's statement except to say, "The only comment is we won't be making any (regulatory) filings until we resolve some issues with them."
Primestar spokeswoman Katie Stephan said she was not aware of any recent conversations with News Corp. "Nothing came of that," she said. "I'm not aware we've been approached again."
DirecTV and Primestar have the lion's share of the direct-broadcast satellite industry's 4.5 million subscribers, with EchoStar far behind.
The News Corp-EchoStar venture was to begin delivering programmes to U.S. households early next year under the News Corp. American Sky Broadcasting name.
EchoStar said in its statement that is has asked for more information from News Corp. about the programme-screening system.

It also said that while it hopes News Corp. will honour its obligations, a new timetable for regulatory filings has not been set and News Corp. may not proceed with its investment. The companies had planned to submit filings to U.S. regulators by the end of April.
EchoStar's class A stock lost $2.375 to close at $14.375 after hitting $13.50, its lowest in more than a year.
News Corp. stock was unchanged at $18.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
